title: Egypt Called This Dam an Existential Threat. Then It Filled.
sources: Every claim is checked against episodes/gerd-nile/research.md (sources, own calculations, both sides of contested points).

Verdict and drought modelling: Wheeler, Whittington, Hall, Murgatroyd, 'Should Egypt be afraid of the GERD?', RiverWare User Group, Feb 2025; Whittington et al. (2025) Water Policy 27(1); Wheeler et al. (2020) Nature Communications 11:5222

Population and electricity access: World Bank SP.POP.TOTL, EG.ELC.ACCS.ZS (CC BY 4.0); per-person share is our calculation (55.5 bn m3 / population)

paragraphs.text: At the start of 2020, this was a quiet river valley in western Ethiopia: dry woodland, low hills, and the Blue Nile winding through the middle. Now watch the same valley, six years later.

That is a brand-new lake, bigger than all of Greater London. It sits behind a wall of concrete a hundred and forty-five metres tall: the Grand Ethiopian Renaissance Dam, the biggest hydropower plant in Africa.

Egypt, more than two and a half thousand kilometres downstream, has called this dam an existential threat. Ethiopia calls it a shared opportunity. Now the lake is full. So what did it actually do to the Nile? And why do the scientists who have modelled this river in detail say the real test hasn't even come yet?
This is the story of a river, two giant dams, and a drought that hasn't happened yet.

shots.subtitle: Egypt, Ethiopia and the future of the Nile

paragraphs.text: To understand why one dam can frighten a country of more than a hundred million people, you have to see the Nile for what it really is. Not one river, but two.

steps.at: you have to see the Nile

paragraphs.text: The first begins near the equator, at Lake Victoria. The White Nile is steady and patient. But on its long way north it crosses the Sudd, one of the biggest wetlands on Earth, where about half of its water simply evaporates.

The second begins in the mountains of Ethiopia, at Lake Tana. The Blue Nile is anything but patient. For most of the year it is a modest river. Then the summer rains hit the highlands, and from July to October it turns into a torrent. The same Ethiopian rivers also carry almost all of the Nile's silt, the mud that once made Egypt's fields so fertile.
The two rivers meet in Khartoum, the capital of Sudan. From there to the Mediterranean, they are simply the Nile.

Now here is the number that explains everything. Add the Blue Nile to two smaller rivers that also come down from the Ethiopian highlands, and you get around eighty-five percent of all the water that reaches Egypt.
More than half of the whole basin's water starts above a single point on the Blue Nile, about fourteen kilometres from the border with Sudan. That point is where Ethiopia built its dam.

shots.on_screen_text: 53% of the basin's water starts upstream of here

paragraphs.text: And Egypt? About ninety-five percent of Egyptians live within twenty kilometres of the river and its delta. And around ninety-seven percent of the country's renewable water comes from outside its borders.

shots.on_screen_text: 95% live within 20 km of the Nile

shots.photo: The Cairo metropolitan area is split by the Nile River at the base of the Nile Delta (iss074e0043697).jpg
shots.on_screen_text: 97% of its water comes from abroad

paragraphs.text: So who should have more say over a river: the country where it rises, or the country that has lived on it for thousands of years? Tell me where you stand in the comments.

ask.text: Who should have more say: where a river rises, or where it's used?

steps.at: or the country that has lived

paragraphs.text: For most of the twentieth century, the answer was written in Cairo. In 1929, an agreement with Britain, which signed for its East African colonies, gave Egypt a veto over new projects upstream.

Thirty years later, in 1959, Egypt and Sudan divided the river between themselves. Of roughly eighty-four billion cubic metres a year, Egypt would take fifty-five and a half, Sudan eighteen and a half, and about ten would be lost to evaporation. Ethiopia got nothing. Ethiopia wasn't in the room.

shots.on_screen_text: 1959: Egypt and Sudan split the Nile

paragraphs.text: Ethiopia has never accepted that deal. In 2024, a separate treaty signed by upstream countries came into force without Egypt or Sudan, which reject it. But the 1959 numbers still sit at the heart of Egypt's case. And they hide something we worked out ourselves.

shots.on_screen_text: Upstream Nile treaty in force: 13 October 2024

paragraphs.text: In 1960, Egypt had about twenty-seven million people. Its fifty-five and a half billion cubic metres came to over two thousand cubic metres of Nile water per person, per year. By 2024, Egypt had more than a hundred and sixteen million people, and the very same share came to about four hundred and seventy-six.

That is below five hundred, the line water experts use for absolute scarcity. The number on paper never changed. The country did. And Egypt had already learned once what happens when the river simply doesn't come.

chapters.title: The Summer the River Almost Stopped

paragraphs.text: Egypt's answer to the Nile's moods was the Aswan High Dam, finished in 1970. Behind it rose Lake Nasser, one of the largest man-made lakes on Earth, big enough to hold about two years of the river's flow.

shots.photo: High Aswan Dam (built to control the Nile floods, store water and produce 2,1 GW of electricity) (14469341352).jpg
Lake Nasser, created by the Aswan High Dam in southern Egypt (iss073e0879542).jpg
shots.on_screen_text: Lake Nasser, seen from the ISS

paragraphs.text: That dam changed history before it was even finished. In 1956, after America and Britain withdrew their offer to help pay for it, President Gamal Abdel Nasser nationalised the Suez Canal, saying its tolls would fund the dam. The Soviet Union stepped in to help build it.

shots.photo: Kosykin (links) bezoekt Egyptes historische schatten, Kosykin (linkls) en Nasser, Bestanddeelnr 919-1605.jpg

paragraphs.text: The new lake swallowed more than four hundred and eighty kilometres of the Nile valley, and the river's yearly flood, which had shaped Egyptian life for thousands of years, stopped reaching the fields downstream. Whole temples had to be cut into blocks and carried uphill, Abu Simbel among them.

shots.photo: Egypt’s Nile River turns into Lake Nasser at the Aswan High Dam (iss074e0315952).jpg
Nubia, Temples of Abu Simbel, Pictures, photo 4 of 7 - Archivio fotografico Museo Egizio, Turin Album2 092.jpg

paragraphs.text: Then the rains failed. Through the 1980s, drought hit the Ethiopian highlands, and the summer flood that Egypt had always counted on kept shrinking. Year after year, Lake Nasser drained.
In 1980, the lake's lowest level of the year was a hundred and seventy-one metres above sea level. By July 1988, it had fallen to a hundred and fifty point six. The lowest ever recorded.

In May that year, President Hosni Mubarak warned that the turbines at the High Dam could stop completely by July if the water kept falling. Then that summer, the rains came back to the highlands, and with them the flood. Egypt had been rescued by the weather.

shots.photo: ISS-64 Aswan Dam and Lake Nasser, Egypt.jpg
shots.on_screen_text: May 1988: a warning from the president

shots.query: heavy rain clouds over green mountains

paragraphs.text: The lesson Egypt drew from 1988 was simple: storage is survival. As long as the river's biggest reserve sits inside Egypt, Egypt holds the Nile's savings account. Now imagine a big part of those savings moving upstream, into someone else's country.

On the second of April 2011, Ethiopia's prime minister, Meles Zenawi, laid the foundation stone. The timing was striking. Less than two months earlier, Egypt's president Hosni Mubarak had been forced from power, and Cairo was consumed by its revolution.

For Ethiopia, the dam was about something very basic. In 2024, according to the World Bank, only a little more than half of Ethiopians had electricity at home. By our count, that leaves about fifty-seven million people without it.

So Ethiopia set out to build the biggest hydropower plant in Africa, and to pay for most of it at home. Civil servants contributed part of their salaries. Ethiopians at home and abroad bought government bonds. The bill came to close to five billion dollars.

The scale is hard to picture. The main wall is a hundred and forty-five metres tall and nearly one point eight kilometres long, and a second rock-fill dam, about five kilometres long, closes a low gap in the hills nearby. Behind them sit seventy-four billion cubic metres of water. That is almost twice what China's Three Gorges Dam holds, and about a year and a half of the Blue Nile's entire flow.

chart.title: Water behind the dam
chart.source: Dam data; Wheeler et al. 2025 (Blue Nile flow at the dam)

paragraphs.text: Its thirteen turbines can produce five thousand one hundred and fifty megawatts, more than doubling Ethiopia's power output, and Ethiopia has signed deals to sell electricity to neighbours such as Kenya.
Here's a question I keep coming back to. If you were Ethiopia, would you have gone ahead without a deal, or waited for one, maybe for decades? Tell me which you'd choose.

ask.text: Build without a deal, or wait for one? What would you have done?

paragraphs.text: Egypt saw it very differently. In June 2013, politicians in Cairo discussed sabotaging the dam in a meeting that, it turned out, was being broadcast live on television. Soon after, President Mohamed Morsi said that all options were open.

shots.author: Mohamed Morsi, President of Egypt, June 2013

paragraphs.text: Two years later, the tone had changed. In March 2015, in Khartoum, the leaders of Egypt, Sudan and Ethiopia signed a Declaration of Principles. The dam should not cause significant harm, and the three countries would cooperate. Then came the hard part: the details.

The details were about water, and time. At talks in Washington in 2019 and 2020, Ethiopia offered to release thirty-five billion cubic metres a year and to fill the lake over five years. Egypt wanted forty billion, and seven years. In February 2020, Ethiopia declined to sign.

In July 2020, as the rainy season began, the filling started anyway. Sudan said the Blue Nile had dropped sharply and that water stations in Khartoum had stopped working. Ethiopia said it had not closed any gates, and that the lake was simply rising with the rain.

shots.photo: Reservoir Filling Behind the Grand Ethiopian Renaissance Dam (CIRA 2025-09-15 - 20200).png

paragraphs.text: The words kept getting harsher. In September 2020, Washington suspended part of its aid to Ethiopia. A month later, the American president said publicly that Egypt might end up blowing up the dam. Ethiopia's prime minister replied that his country would not cave in to aggression. In 2021, an adviser to Sudan's leader spoke of a possible water war, and that July the dispute reached the UN Security Council. In 2023, Egypt and Sudan held joint military exercises. And in December of that year, the last formal round of talks collapsed, with each side blaming the other.
On the ninth of September 2025, with the lake full, Ethiopia formally opened the dam. Its prime minister called it not a threat, but a shared opportunity. Egypt protested to the United Nations.

So, five fillings later, what actually happened? Here is the new lake rising, year by year: about five hundred and forty metres above sea level in 2020, six hundred in 2022, and six hundred and forty, completely full, by late 2024.

And downstream? A team of researchers, including hydrologists at the University of Oxford, spent years building a detailed model of the Eastern Nile together with engineers from the Nile countries. Looking back in 2025, their verdict was clear: the filling did not cause appreciable harm to Egypt.

shots.photo: Reservoir Filling Behind the Grand Ethiopian Renaissance Dam (CIRA 2025-09-15 - 20220).png
Reservoir Filling Behind the Grand Ethiopian Renaissance Dam (CIRA 2025-09-15 - 20240).png

paragraphs.text: Why? Partly luck: the filling years brought strong floods. And partly planning: Egypt had built up its reserves in Lake Nasser ahead of time. Today both lakes are full, and the researchers call it the new normal.

shots.on_screen_text: Both reservoirs full: the new normal

paragraphs.text: Ethiopia, meanwhile, got what it built the dam for. The first turbine started sending power to the grid in February 2022, and more have come online ever since.

Sudan, caught in between, may gain the most: steadier flows, fewer destructive floods, more irrigation, less silt clogging its own dams, cheaper power. But only if the releases upstream are coordinated.

In late September 2025, just weeks after the opening, Sudan was hit by severe Nile floods. Egypt called it a man-made flood, caused by sudden releases from the dam. Ethiopia said the floods had nothing to do with the dam, and that without it they would have been far worse. Sudan called for a joint review. That argument has not been settled.
So, what do you think? Did the dam cause those floods, or soften them? I'd really like to hear your reasoning.

ask.text: Did the dam cause the 2025 floods, or soften them?

shots.on_screen_text: Khartoum: where the two Niles meet

paragraphs.text: We'll keep following this river into the dry years, so if you want to see how this story ends, subscribe.
Because the real test is still ahead. History says the Nile will, sooner or later, have another run of dry years like the 1980s. What happens then?

The same researchers ran the river through a hundred simulated futures, plus a replay of the 1980s drought. They even tested a scenario they stress is purely hypothetical: an Ethiopia that runs the dam on purpose to hurt Egypt. Even then, the chance that Egypt would have to cut its water deliveries in any given year stayed below seven percent.

shots.on_screen_text: Shortage risk for Egypt: low, even in the worst case

paragraphs.text: Hurting Egypt would also cost Ethiopia dearly. Water held back is water that doesn't spin its turbines, which is why the researchers found Ethiopia would have very little financial reason to try.

shots.at: which is why the researchers found

paragraphs.text: In their models, one of the most delicate moments is the end of a long drought, when both lakes are low and both need the same returning water. Their compromise scenario has Ethiopia release extra water in the dry years, then refill in step with Egypt. Egypt already has drought rules of its own: as Lake Nasser's storage falls below sixty, fifty-five and fifty billion cubic metres, releases are cut by five, ten and fifteen percent. What doesn't exist is any agreement on what Ethiopia does in those years.

chart.title: Egypt's own drought rule
chart.source: Release cuts at the High Dam, as modelled by Wheeler et al. 2025

paragraphs.text: What would such rules look like? Researchers have been sketching them for years: share real-time data on both reservoirs, agree in advance how much extra water flows downstream when a drought drags on, and agree how both lakes refill once the rain returns. None of that requires pulling anything down. It requires trust.

shots.quote: Management of multi-year droughts will require careful coordination if risks of harmful impacts are to be minimized.
shots.author: Wheeler et al., Nature Communications, 2020

paragraphs.text: Egypt isn't simply waiting. At Bahr el-Baqar it has built what Guinness lists as the world's largest wastewater treatment plant, cleaning five point six million cubic metres a day to farm the desert in Sinai. And in a project called the New Delta, it is turning more desert green. Here it is in 2018, and again in 2024.

shots.at: to farm the desert in Sinai
a project called the New Delta
shots.photo: A “New Delta” in the Desert (153752 - 20181128 lrg).jpg
A “New Delta” in the Desert (153752 - 2 20241120 lrg).jpg

paragraphs.text: So, was the dam the catastrophe Egypt feared? So far, the evidence says no. Did it change the Nile forever? Yes. For the first time, a big part of the river's savings sits upstream, in Ethiopia. The concrete is finished. The lake is full. What hasn't been built yet is the one thing that matters most in the dry years: a set of rules that both countries trust.

steps.at: Did it change the Nile forever

paragraphs.text: When the next long drought comes, will the Nile have rules, or a crisis? Leave your prediction in the comments. I'll be reading them.

ask.text: When the next drought comes: rules, or a crisis?

youtube.description:
In 2020 it was a river valley in western Ethiopia. Today it is a lake bigger than Greater London. Africa's biggest hydropower dam is finished and full, so what did it really do to the Nile, and why do the researchers who modelled the river say the real test hasn't come yet?

Real Copernicus Sentinel-2 satellite images, NASA archive photos, World Bank data and our own calculations.
